title: Love Forbidden
full_review:
An emotionally fragile young French filmmaker attending a yearlong seminar in Rome finds himself obsessed with a bisexual Italian writer also attending the workshop in the leaden, gay-themed thriller "Love Forbidden" (Strand).Shot on video, director Rodolphe Marconi's torpid meditation on desire feels -- and looks -- like a student film, its narrative wandering aimlessly rather than moving chillingly toward its potboiler climax.

The focus of this unfocused tale is Bruce (played by Marconi), a brooding Parisian haunted by the death of his novelist brother, who travels to Rome to spend a year as artist-in-residence at the palatial Medici Villa. Estranged from his parents, and having recently broken up with his girlfriend, Bruce is a study in loneliness.

That all changes when he meets the villa's Sicilian office intern, Matteo (Andrea Necci), a sometime writer, sometime philosopher and all-times stud who gives Bruce a personal tour of the Eternal City. Though confused at first about his feelings for Matteo, Bruce quickly falls under his intoxicating influence. They end up spending a night together.

But no sooner does Bruce surrender to passion than Matteo pulls the emotional carpet out from under his feet by starting a heterosexual relationship with an American tart (Echo Danon) who is writing a book about serial killers.

Unable to break free of Matteo's gravitational pull, Bruce's delicate psyche begins to fracture, propelling the story to its incoherent conclusion.

Far from being an erotic thriller, Marconi's film lacks suspense, unfolding more like a cheesy movie-of-the-week -- even if the cheese used is brie. Yet far more off-putting than the flick's interminable pacing, impassive performances or amateurish bargain-basement look is the problematic sexual ambiguity of its characters. Marconi never definitively establishes their orientation, opting to present a more malleable concept of sexuality, one which remains open to the prevailing -- and fickle -- winds of lust.

Apart from its morally disagreeable elements, "Love Forbidden" is weighed down by poorly lit, shaky hand-held shots of Roman nightlife and tedious cutaways of Renaissance art, which feel like padding and betray the underlying poverty of the script. Marconi tries to draw not-so-subtle homoerotic parallels by inter-cutting the lovers' nocturnal frolicking with images of semi-nude Roman sculptures.

The narrative is saddled with insufferable sequences consisting of Bruce moping around Medici Villa, smoking a cigarette or staring listlessly at his bedroom ceiling, which, from the audience's standpoint, is akin to being forced to watch corn grow.

Late in the game, Bruce confides to his diary that he longs to "fly far away" from his misery. By that point so do the viewers.

Subtitles.

Due to a few homosexual encounters and an implied heterosexual tryst, as well as recurring rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
